prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

cymothoa exigua*: the tongue as what it is not—blemish and parasite: gimp and glottal stop: what question can be answered with a truant mouth: can the lynched man hung from the sails of a windmill taste the lead pipe wedged between his lips: when the signifiers dangle, empty chum lines in a cold creek: when the men in Waco, wearing white straw hats, fraying at the crisp edges of their white shirts, leave Jesse, leave John, leave Paul in ashes in the unpaved streets to choke passing mules into prophecy: when we pinch our noses to staunch the smell of the twice burnt black man burning for a third time this day: when the boys, sweet and good animals, come to what’s been left in shallow ditches: false rib and femur, clavicle and severed hand—quite simply, the language of sorrow: glyph of the gadfly rooting himself into the rotting meat of the dead: when it is too late to refuse our bodies being made urns: corn, unharvested and heavy in its husks: when, in the marketplace, the butcher lifts our tongue from a bed of ice, shouts: who will speak for this flesh: when the tongue answers as all severed tongues do:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Waco, Jesse, John

outputs.L1: *Cymothoa exigua*: the tongue as what it is not—blemish and parasite; gimp and glottal stop. What question can be answered with a truant mouth? Can the lynched man, hung from the sails of a windmill, taste the lead pipe wedged between his lips? When the signifiers dangle—empty chum lines in a cold creek; when the men in Waco, wearing white straw hats, the crisp edges of their white shirts fraying, leave Jesse, leave John, leave Paul in ashes in the unpaved streets to choke passing mules into prophecy; when we pinch our noses to staunch the smell of the twice-burnt Black man burning for a third time this day; when the boys, sweet and good animals, come upon what has been left in shallow ditches: false rib and femur, clavicle and severed hand—quite simply, the language of sorrow; glyph of the gadfly rooting himself into the rotting meat of the dead; when it is too late to refuse our bodies being made urns; corn, unharvested and heavy in its husks; when, in the marketplace, the butcher lifts our tongue from a bed of ice and shouts, “Who will speak for this flesh?”; when the tongue answers as all severed tongues do:
outputs.L2: *cymothoa exigua*: the tongue understood through everything it is denied to be—scar, infestation: limp, interruption in the throat: what kind of answer can come from a mouth gone absent without leave: can the lynched man, suspended from the blades of a windmill, still taste the lead pipe forced between his lips: when words hang loose, like baitless lines over a winter creek: when the men in Waco, white straw hats on their heads, the sharp borders of their white shirts beginning to unravel, abandon Jesse, abandon John, abandon Paul as ash in the dirt roads, left to make passing mules cough themselves into omen: when we hold our noses against the stench of the Black man burned twice already and burning yet again today: when the boys, gentle and obedient creatures, arrive at what remains in the shallow trenches: a false rib, a thighbone, a collarbone, a hand cut away—nothing less than grief made into speech: the mark of the biting fly burrowing into the decaying flesh of the dead: when refusal comes too late, and our bodies have already been turned into vessels for ashes: corn standing uncut, swollen and weighted inside its husks: when, at the market, the butcher raises our tongue from its ice-packed tray and cries out: who is going to give voice to this meat: when the tongue replies in the only manner a severed tongue can:
outputs.L3:
The poem presents the tongue as both a damaged organ and a parasite, using this disturbing image to question the limits of speech and expression. Rather than treating the tongue simply as an instrument of voice, the poem imagines it as something wounded, detached, and almost alien to the body. This creates a sense that language itself has been injured. Speech is not shown as whole or free, but as something marked by pain, violence, and survival. By making the tongue both part of the body and something that feeds on or clings to it, the poem suggests that expression can be inseparable from suffering.

The imagery of lynching, burning, and mutilation evokes the historical violence inflicted on Black bodies. These images call up a legacy of racial terror in which the body is not only killed but publicly destroyed, displayed, and dehumanized. The poem’s violence is therefore not abstract. It is rooted in history and in the physical realities of anti-Black brutality. Through references to bodily harm, the poem forces the reader to confront the ways in which racism has attempted to silence Black people by attacking their bodies, their voices, and their ability to be remembered as fully human.

At the same time, the poem connects bodily remains with language. The damaged body becomes a kind of text, and sorrow itself becomes a form of testimony. Even when ordinary speech is impossible, grief communicates. The remains of the body carry meaning, bearing the marks of what has happened. In this way, the poem suggests that violence leaves behind evidence that cannot be entirely erased. The body, even in fragments, speaks through its wounds.

This raises one of the poem’s central questions: who can speak for the dead when their bodies and voices have been severed? If the tongue has been cut out, if the body has been burned or broken, then conventional speech is no longer possible. Yet the need for witness remains. The poem explores the difficulty of representing those who have been violently silenced without claiming to fully possess their voices. It asks how memory, mourning, and poetry might respond to histories in which the dead were denied the chance to speak for themselves.

The final image of the severed tongue powerfully suggests that even silenced flesh bears witness to violence. Although the tongue can no longer speak in the usual sense, its very severing becomes evidence. Its muteness is not empty; it testifies to the brutality that produced it. The poem therefore transforms silence into a form of witness. It shows that where speech has been destroyed, the wounded body still communicates, insisting that historical violence be seen, remembered, and answered.
outputs.L4:
The text confronts the history of racial terror by presenting lynching not as a distant or abstract atrocity, but as an assault on the body, on language, and on memory. Its poetic method is dense and fragmented: images appear in broken pieces, like the damaged bodies it describes, and anatomical details force the reader to face the physical reality of violence. Flesh, mouths, tongues, wounds, and severed parts become central figures in the work. This emphasis on the body resists any attempt to make racial violence seem clean, symbolic, or safely historical. Instead, the text insists on the material horror of bodily desecration and on the lasting grief carried by those who survive or inherit its memory.

The metaphor of the parasite and the tongue deepens this meditation on violence and speech. The tongue usually represents voice, testimony, and human expression, but here it is threatened, cut, consumed, or transformed. The parasite suggests an invading force that feeds on the body, just as racial terror feeds on Black suffering and attempts to destroy Black personhood. Yet the image is not only one of destruction. Even when the tongue is severed or speech is denied, something remains capable of communication. The damaged body itself becomes a kind of text. Its wounds, silences, and fragments bear witness to what has been done.

In this way, the text turns bodily violation into a language of sorrow and historical testimony. It shows that racist violence tries not only to kill, but also to erase: to silence the victim, to deny the crime, and to make the suffering disappear from public memory. However, the poem refuses that erasure. Its fractured language imitates the effects of trauma while also preserving the evidence of it. The broken images do not signal failure; they become a form of witness. The body, even in pain and dismemberment, continues to speak.

Ultimately, the text suggests that when ordinary human speech has been violently suppressed, the flesh itself becomes eloquent. The violated body carries memory, grief, accusation, and truth. Through its difficult poetic form, the work forces readers to encounter the afterlife of lynching and racial terror, while also honoring the persistence of testimony under conditions meant to make testimony impossible. It transforms silence into expression and desecrated flesh into a powerful language of mourning and resistance.
outputs.L5:
In Waco, the hot Texas sun seemed to slow everything down, from the traffic on the wide roads to the conversations on shaded front porches. Jesse had lived there his whole life and knew every backstreet, diner, and dusty field on the edge of town. To him, Waco was more than a place on a map—it was a collection of memories.

John arrived in Waco one summer afternoon with a suitcase, a notebook, and no real plan. He met Jesse at a small coffee shop near the river, where Jesse was fixing an old guitar with the patience of someone who had learned not to rush life. The two began talking, first about music, then about family, and finally about the strange ways people end up exactly where they need to be.

Over the following weeks, Jesse showed John the city: the bridges over the Brazos River, the quiet streets at sunset, and the places only locals seemed to know. John, in return, helped Jesse see Waco differently—not just as home, but as a place full of stories waiting to be told.

By the end of the summer, Jesse and John had become close friends. Waco had given them both something they needed: for Jesse, a renewed love for the familiar; for John, a sense of belonging he had been searching for all along.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense experimental prose poem beginning with “cymothoa exigua” that uses the tongue-eating louse as a metaphor for stolen speech, racial terror, lynching, and the body as archive.
counterfactuals.output:
cymothoa exigua enters through the gill like a rumor with legs, clamps the pink hymn-muscle, drinks until the tongue is a husk, then takes its place and speaks fish for the fish. Say: parasite, but mean empire. Say: mouth, but mean courthouse, classroom, checkpoint, auction block, newsprint, tree. The stolen organ does not vanish; it becomes evidence in the belly of the thief, a wet archive, a grammar of bruises. Every syllable they took still twitches under the floorboards of the nation.

I have seen a body made into a document without consent: rope-script at the neck, ash-margin, photograph passed hand to hand like a public prayer. I have seen terror punctuate the air where language should have been. The crowd called it justice and the camera called it memory and the caption called it unidentified, but the body knew its own name, kept it under the tongue that was not there, kept it in the teeth, in the bitten cheek, in the salt vault of blood. What is a throat after the song is confiscated? A tunnel full of witnesses. What is skin? A page that outlives the fire.

The louse speaks from inside the wound: I am your new vocabulary. I will pronounce you harmless. I will translate your screaming into weather. I will make your mother’s grief sound like statistics. I will make the tree innocent, the knot innocent, the sheriff only standing nearby, the boys only boys, the postcard only paper, the silence only time passing. But beneath that counterfeit tongue, another tongue roots downward, black and fibrous, feeding on iron, on dirt, on the names carved into no stone. It learns to speak in scars. It conjugates survival: I was, I am, I been, I be.

O archive-body, O dark ledger breathing, open your ribbed shelves. Show us the cotton lodged in the lung, the river carrying its inventory of bones, the hymn with a split lip, the child taught to swallow questions before they attract dogs. Show us how memory hides in the joints when the mouth is occupied. How the grandmother’s pause is a museum. How the son’s flinch is a footnote. How the daughter braids a map into her hair and calls it pretty so the empire will not confiscate that too.

There are creatures that survive by becoming the missing part. There are nations that survive by calling the missing part a myth. But at night the borrowed tongue loosens. It cannot hold the dead down. They rise not as ghosts but as syntax: a long black sentence refusing its period, a choir of cut throats humming through the parasite’s mouth, making of its theft an instrument, making of the wound a door, making of the body not a crime scene only, not a relic only, but a living archive that opens, and opens, and opens, saying: we were never speechless; you were only standing on our tongues.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-sentence lyric essay fragment in a contemporary avant-garde style about the tongue, parasitism, and the Waco lynching of Jesse Washington, using visceral imagery and rhetorical questions.
counterfactuals.output: What is the tongue if not a borrowed parasite in the mouth—wet witness, root-fed and trembling—asking how a town could gather in Waco around Jesse Washington’s burning body and call the spectacle justice, asking what sweetness remained in the air afterward, what language survived with soot under its nails?

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark, surreal poem with no clear ending, centered on severed tongues, signifiers, Black suffering, and the question “who will speak for this flesh?”
counterfactuals.output:
In the archive of midnight,  
tongues hang like blackened bells,  
unrung,  
their roots still dreaming of mouths.

A hand labels each silence:  
evidence,  
riot,  
body,  
song—  
signifiers pinned to the velvet wall  
where history keeps its insects.

Somewhere a child learns  
that grief has a grammar  
older than the whip,  
older than the ship’s wet teeth,  
older than the auction block  
where names were broken into coins.

The severed tongues keep moving.

They spell no word we can keep.  
They curl around smoke,  
around cotton ghosts,  
around the red hymn  
of knees in the street,  
around mothers who wake  
with sirens nesting in their throats.

Who will speak for this flesh?

Not the law,  
with its mouth full of keys.  
Not the camera,  
drinking and drinking.  
Not the monument,  
stone-faced beneath its birdshit crown.

The flesh speaks in bruised constellations,  
in the blue hour between bullet and headline,  
in the hush after the verdict  
when even God seems to be reading  
from a torn script.

Still, the tongues gather—  
under doors,  
inside drums,  
beneath the polished table  
where the living are translated  
into statistics.

They whisper from the salt.  
They whisper from the blood-dark river.  
They whisper from the wound  
that refuses to become metaphor.

And the signifiers multiply:  
shadow,  
property,  
threat,  
martyr,  
absence,  
fuel.

Each word a mask.  
Each mask a cage.  
Each cage singing softly  
with someone else’s breath.

Who will speak for this flesh?

The night opens its many mouths.  
No answer comes clean.  
Only the severed tongues,  
wet with ancestral thunder,  
crawling back toward the body—  
not to be healed,  
not to be named,  
but to tremble  
at the edge of speech,

where a scream becomes a door,

where the door becomes water,

where the water remembers,

where the remembering begins to say—
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a horrifying poetic passage that blends biological parasitism, anatomy, language theory, and historical lynching imagery—make it fragmented, biblical, and grief-stricken.
counterfactuals.output:
And the word entered the body and found there a host.

Not spirit. Not metaphor. A mouth.

It fastened beneath the tongue like a white larva, feeding on salt, on milk-teeth, on the little grammar of breathing. It learned the throat’s dark corridor, the cartilage gates, the red cathedral of the lungs opening and closing like torn scripture.

And lo, the body was named.

Named until it bent.

Named until the skin became a document others claimed to read.

In the beginning was the sign, and the sign was against us, and the sign hung over the road. A syllable nailed to a tree. A crowd beneath it, speaking in one fevered grammar, their faces lifted as if toward weather, as if toward God.

But God had gone into the weeds.

God had gone into the flies.

God had gone into the mother’s hands, empty and shaking.

See: the parasite does not merely consume. It revises. It enters the blood and changes the hymn. It teaches the nerve to misfire, the eye to expect rope in every line of horizon, the ear to hear verdict in every pronoun.

A body can be made into a sentence.

A sentence can be made into a noose.

O children of dust and alphabet, who taught you that naming was innocence?

Who taught you the lexicon of the mob—the hot consonants, the spit-bright vowels, the holy book misquoted under lantern-light?

There was a tree.

There was always a tree.

Its roots drank rain, iron, rumor. Its branches carried birds until men made it carry testimony. The leaves trembled, not from wind, but from the burden of being made witness.

And the town slept afterward.

The town washed its hands in daylight.

The town conjugated mercy in the past tense.

I have seen language crawl from the wound with mandibles of law. I have seen anatomy become evidence: skull, wrist, rib, the blue map of veins beneath beloved skin. I have seen grief open the chest and find no organ for justice, only the heart, that exhausted animal, still knocking.

Mother, behold thy son.

Son, behold the grammar they built for your vanishing.

No elegy is clean. It comes with soil under its nails. It comes infected. It carries the eggs of old speech, waiting to hatch in the next mouth, the next classroom, the next courthouse, the next soft prayer said by someone who does not know what history has laid beneath the tongue.

Break the word.

Break the branch.

Break the sermon that blessed the swarm.

Yet still—

beneath the ruined syntax,

beneath the blackened page,

beneath the ribs where sorrow nests and feeds,

there remains a breath.

Small.

Unowned.

Refusing translation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of an experimental elegy: start with “cymothoa exigua*:” and explore the tongue as parasite, wound, witness, and failed instrument of speech, incorporating Waco, ashes, bone, corn, and a butcher’s marketplace.
counterfactuals.output:
cymothoa exigua*:

the tongue enters first as a hunger,  
then as a replacement for hunger.

It fastens to the wound of speech  
and drinks until speech is pale,  
until the mouth forgets  
what belonged there before.

O little butcher of the wet cathedral,  
O pink clerk in the marketplace of teeth,  
you weigh the syllables on a hook,  
you hang them beside the lamb shanks,  
the blue-veined liver,  
the corn still furred with field-dust.

Who taught you witness?  
Was it Waco burning through the screen,  
ash lifting its gray alphabet  
over the bones of the unnamed?  
Was it the mother with smoke in her hair  
calling a child’s name  
until the name became a coal  
and the coal became a seed  
and the seed refused the earth?

The tongue says: I was there.  
The tongue says: I tasted plaster, hymnbook, siren, milk.  
The tongue says nothing—  
having been eaten by its own testimony.

In the butcher’s marketplace  
the knives shine like small doctrines.  
Every stall offers a method  
for dividing the living from the livable.  
Here is bone, white and instructional.  
Here is ash, sifted for proof.  
Here is corn, gold teeth of the field,  
ground down to meal, to bread, to body,  
to something a mouth can fail to bless.

And the parasite, enthroned in the absence,  
moves when the host would speak.

It is almost a tongue.  
It is almost mercy.  
It shapes the wound into an organ  
and calls that music.

But listen:  
beneath the salt-click, beneath the market’s flies,  
beneath the elegy’s black apron,  
there is a silence with roots.

It grows through bone.  
It tassels in the corn.  
It settles on Waco as ash,  
not to cover,  
not to forgive,  
but to remain.

The mouth opens.

A witness crawls out.

No word survives it whole.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
